messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Thanks to devtools, I have developed my fiirst package: A library of helpers for doing SEM with OpenMx

https://github.com/tbates/umx

It's running well for me, and for install_github(tbates/umx) users on mac.

Just had my first PC user... they just can't get it to run.

It's just source R files, with roxygen help. No C/Fortran etc, so, some questions:

1. How can one release binary packages at github (to avoid the need for users to have compile tools)
2. How can one create windows and *nix binary packages from a mac?
3. Why can't a PC user install packages from source when a mac user can?
4. If  one pushes a package to CRAN, is it frowned on to then push updates often?

many thanks, t

It is so helpful to be able to just say
devtools::document("~/bin/umx"); devtools::install("~/bin/umx"); devtools::build("~/bin/umx")

Is it possible to tell build() to push the file to github, replacing the file of the same name in the most recent download?

This would mean that a call to install_github("tbates/umx") always pulled what the developer had last built, without the developer needing to go to github pages and point and click and drag and drop (even though this rocks, it gets a bit tedious if you are fixing/pushing things a couple of times a day

thanks again for a cool tool!

t

> Hi Winston,

It is the case -- install_github grabs the zip file which contains all the files from master (or other branch/tag, if specified). It's the same as if you click the "Download ZIP" button on the project page. The zip file is automatically generated by Github. Then it's built and installed on the user's machine.

-Winston

I think Timothy's interested in distributing binary builds via github.
 This is certainly possible to do (and would be relatively easy to
automate in devtools), but I don't think it's the right approach.
It's not clear exactly what the right approach is yet, but I suspect
it involves checking and building on https://travis-ci.org/, then
uploading the binary artifact to a hosting service (probably s3), then
either constructing the appropriate url, or using a webserver to
provide an overlay that mimics the usual R repo structure.

Hadley
